reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: The commonest soft-tissue sarcoma of childhood, with the embryonal subtype predominating in young children and the alveolar subtype more common in older children and adolescents
Site varies with subtype: head and neck (including orbit and parameningeal), genitourinary tract, and extremities are typical, and presentation reflects local mass effect
The botryoid variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma forms grape-like polypoid masses in hollow, mucosa-lined organs such as the vagina or bladder
Fusion status is prognostically decisive: PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusion-positive tumours (usually alveolar morphology) behave more aggressively than fusion-negative tumours
Diagnosis rests on skeletal muscle differentiation shown by desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1 immunohistochemistry alongside morphology and molecular testing
Treatment is risk-stratified multimodality therapy combining multi-agent chemotherapy with surgery and/or radiotherapy for local control
Parameningeal tumours can extend intracranially and require careful evaluation for meningeal and central nervous system involvement
Staging includes primary-site MRI, regional nodal assessment, chest CT, whole-body functional imaging, and bone-marrow examination
reference.pathophysiology: Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignancy of primitive mesenchymal cells committed to skeletal muscle differentiation but arrested before maturation. The alveolar subtype is characteristically driven by a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusion gene that generates a potent chimeric transcription factor promoting proliferation and blocking myogenic maturation. Embryonal tumours generally lack these fusions and instead show a range of alterations, frequently involving the RAS pathway and loss of imprinting at chromosome 11p15. Because fusion status correlates better with behaviour than morphology alone, molecular classification into fusion-positive and fusion-negative disease now guides risk assessment.
additionalDifferentials: Ewing sarcoma and other small round cell tumours
Infantile fibrosarcoma and other paediatric spindle-cell tumours
Benign lesions such as haemangioma or lymphangioma at soft-tissue sites
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to delineate extent and relation to critical structures
Whole-body functional imaging for nodal and distant staging
Bone-marrow aspirate and trephine to detect marrow involvement
Lumbar puncture and dedicated neuroimaging for parameningeal tumours to assess central nervous system spread
Biopsy with immunohistochemistry (desmin, myogenin, MyoD1) and molecular testing for FOXO1 fusions
redFlags: A parameningeal tumour with cranial nerve palsies, headache, or signs of intracranial extension
Rapidly growing painless mass in a child, especially at head and neck or genitourinary sites
Airway or urinary obstruction from a botryoid or pelvic mass
Features of disseminated disease such as bone pain or cytopenias suggesting marrow involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by fusion status, stage and clinical group, primary site, patient age, and histological subtype; localised, fusion-negative embryonal tumours at favourable sites do well, whereas fusion-positive, metastatic, or unfavourable-site disease carries a substantially worse outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming morphology alone predicts behaviour rather than confirming fusion status by molecular testing
Underestimating central nervous system risk in parameningeal disease and omitting appropriate neuraxis staging
Inadequate biopsy planning that jeopardises subsequent local control
Overlooking regional lymph node assessment, which is particularly important at extremity and paratesticular sites
Neglecting long-term surveillance for late effects of chemotherapy and radiotherapy in survivors
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Deliver risk-stratified multi-agent chemotherapy, typically vincristine, actinomycin D and cyclophosphamide, as the backbone of treatment
Achieve local control with surgical resection and/or radiotherapy according to site and resectability
Stratify risk by fusion status (PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1), stage, clinical group, primary site and histology to guide treatment intensity
Confirm the diagnosis with immunohistochemistry for desmin, myogenin and MyoD1 alongside molecular testing for FOXO1 fusions
Stage fully with primary-site MRI, chest CT, functional whole-body imaging and marrow examination, adding CSF analysis and neuroimaging for parameningeal tumours
Provide multidisciplinary paediatric and sarcoma oncology care with supportive management of chemotherapy toxicity
Arrange long-term surveillance for relapse and for the late effects of therapy
